name: Niobium
nameMeaning: After Niobe, daughter of Tantalus in Greek myth

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Niobium is a soft gray metal that becomes a superconductor when it gets very cold, carrying electricity with absolutely no loss. That is why niobium wire coils the giant magnets inside MRI scanners and the Large Hadron Collider. It also grows rainbow colors when you pass electricity through it.
funFacts: Niobium jewelry comes in rainbow colors made without any dye — just electricity.
The magnets in MRI scanners are wound with niobium superconducting wire.
The Large Hadron Collider uses tons of niobium to steer particle beams.
It was confused with tantalum for 50 years because the two are so alike.
A pinch of niobium makes pipeline steel much stronger without adding weight.

compounds.name: Niobium pentoxide
compounds.about: Used in special lenses and capacitors.

compounds.name: Columbite
compounds.about: The main niobium ore, part of 'coltan'.

compounds.name: Lithium niobate
compounds.about: Steers laser light in fiber-optic networks.

compounds.name: Niobium carbide
compounds.about: An extremely hard coating for cutting tools.

compounds.name: Niobium-tin
compounds.about: A superconductor for the strongest magnets built.

compounds.name: Niobium-titanium
compounds.about: The superconducting wire in most MRI machines.

compounds.name: Niobium pentachloride
compounds.about: Used to make pure niobium metal.

compounds.name: Niobium nitride
compounds.about: Used in ultra-sensitive light detectors.

compounds.name: Niobium diselenide
compounds.about: A layered crystal studied in nanoscience.

compounds.name: Potassium niobate
compounds.about: Changes laser colors in optical devices.

name: Molybdenum
nameMeaning: From Greek molybdos, 'lead' (it was mistaken for lead)

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Molybdenum has one of the highest melting points of any metal, so it keeps its strength when things get red hot — perfect for jet engines and furnace parts. It is also essential to life: bacteria use molybdenum to pull nitrogen out of the air so plants can grow.
funFacts: Molybdenum does not melt until 2,623 °C.
Its ore is so soft and gray that people mistook it for lead for centuries.
Molybdenum disulfide is slippery like graphite and is used as a dry lubricant.
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria need molybdenum, so life on land depends on it.
German tanks in World War I used molybdenum steel armor.

compounds.name: Molybdenite
compounds.about: The main ore, and a super-slippery dry lubricant.

compounds.name: Molybdenum trioxide
compounds.about: A yellow powder used to make the metal and as a catalyst.

compounds.name: Wulfenite
compounds.about: A striking orange crystal mineral.

compounds.name: Sodium molybdate
compounds.about: A fertilizer and a rust inhibitor.

compounds.name: Molybdenum carbide
compounds.about: A very hard material used in cutting tools.

compounds.name: Ammonium molybdate
compounds.about: Used in lab tests to detect phosphates.

compounds.name: Molybdenum disilicide
compounds.about: Heating elements that glow white hot in furnaces.

compounds.name: Molybdenum hexafluoride
compounds.about: A liquid used to lay down metal films on chips.

compounds.name: Molybdenum pentachloride
compounds.about: A dark green solid used in chemical synthesis.

compounds.name: Molybdenum dioxide
compounds.about: A brown solid used as a catalyst.

name: Technetium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Technetium was the first element ever made by humans rather than found in nature — its name literally means 'artificial'. Every atom of it is radioactive, so any that existed when Earth formed has long since decayed away. Today it is a hospital hero, lighting up scans of bones and hearts.
funFacts: Technetium was the first element created artificially, in 1937.
It left a stubborn gap in Mendeleev's table that nobody could fill for 60 years.
About 30 million medical scans a year use technetium-99m.
Its half-life is only 6 hours in medical use, so it leaves the body quickly.
Astronomers have spotted technetium in certain stars, proving stars are still making elements.

compounds.name: Pertechnetate ion
compounds.about: The form injected for medical scans of the thyroid.

compounds.name: Technetium heptoxide
compounds.about: A yellow solid, the highest oxide of technetium.

compounds.name: Technetium dioxide
compounds.about: A black solid formed when technetium is oxidized.

compounds.name: Sodium pertechnetate
compounds.about: The exact chemical used in hospital imaging kits.

compounds.name: Technetium sulfide
compounds.about: Formed when technetium is precipitated from solution.

compounds.name: Technetium tetrachloride
compounds.about: A red-brown solid studied by chemists.

compounds.name: Pertechnetic acid
compounds.about: A strong acid form of technetium.

compounds.name: Technetium hexafluoride
compounds.about: A golden-yellow volatile solid.

compounds.name: Technetium carbonyl
compounds.about: Used to build medical imaging molecules.

compounds.name: Technetium hydride ion
compounds.about: An unusual ion with nine hydrogen atoms attached.

compoundsNote: Technetium is radioactive and made only in reactors and laboratories, so its compounds are studied by specialists rather than used in everyday life.

name: Ruthenium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Ruthenium is one of the rare platinum metals, and just a tiny sprinkle of it makes other metals far tougher. It is a champion at speeding up chemical reactions, and its compounds are being used to build solar cells that soak up sunlight like a plant leaf.
funFacts: Adding 0.1% ruthenium makes titanium a hundred times more resistant to corrosion.
Ruthenium is one of the rarest metals in the Earth's crust.
The tips of some fancy fountain pen nibs are ruthenium alloy.
Ruthenium dyes power experimental solar cells that mimic photosynthesis.
It won a share of the 2005 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its role as a catalyst.

compounds.name: Ruthenium dioxide
compounds.about: Conducts electricity; used in tiny resistors in electronics.

compounds.name: Ruthenium tetroxide
compounds.about: A volatile yellow solid used to reveal fingerprints.

compounds.name: Ruthenium chloride
compounds.about: The starting point for most ruthenium chemistry.

compounds.name: Ruthenium bipyridine
compounds.about: Glows orange under light; used in solar cell research.

compounds.name: Strontium ruthenate
compounds.about: A metallic oxide used in electronic devices.

compounds.name: Grubbs catalyst
compounds.about: A Nobel-winning ruthenium tool for building new molecules.

compounds.name: Laurite
compounds.about: The rare mineral in which ruthenium is found.

compounds.name: Triruthenium dodecacarbonyl
compounds.about: An orange cluster compound used in catalysis.

compounds.name: Ruthenium hexafluoride
compounds.about: A dark brown, very reactive solid.

compounds.name: Potassium ruthenate
compounds.about: An orange salt used as an oxidizing agent.

name: Rhodium
nameMeaning: From Greek rhodon, 'rose', for its pink salts

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Rhodium is the most expensive precious metal in the world — often worth many times more than gold. It is brilliantly shiny and never tarnishes, so white gold jewelry is plated with it. Almost all rhodium goes into car exhausts, where it cleans harmful gases out of the fumes.
funFacts: Rhodium has at times been worth more than ten times the price of gold.
Around 80% of all rhodium ends up in car catalytic converters.
Most 'white gold' rings are actually plated with rhodium to look bright white.
It is one of the rarest elements in the Earth's crust.
Guinness World Records once gave Paul McCartney a rhodium-plated disc.

compounds.name: Rhodium chloride
compounds.about: The most common rhodium chemical, dark red in color.

compounds.name: Rhodium oxide
compounds.about: A gray-black solid used in catalysts.

compounds.name: Wilkinson's catalyst
compounds.about: A famous rhodium tool for adding hydrogen to molecules.

compounds.name: Rhodium dicarbonyl
compounds.about: Used to make many everyday chemicals.

compounds.name: Rhodium acetate
compounds.about: A green dimer used in advanced organic chemistry.

compounds.name: Rhodium hexafluoride
compounds.about: A black, extremely reactive solid.

compounds.name: Sodium hexachlororhodate
compounds.about: Used in rhodium plating baths.

compounds.name: Rhodium sulfide
compounds.about: A catalyst that resists chemical poisoning.

compounds.name: Rhodium hydride
compounds.about: An intermediate step in hydrogen-adding reactions.

compounds.name: Ammonium hexachlororhodate
compounds.about: A step in purifying rhodium from ore.

name: Palladium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Palladium has an amazing party trick: it can soak up 900 times its own volume in hydrogen gas, like a metal sponge. It is a superb catalyst, cleaning up car exhaust fumes and helping chemists build medicines. It is named after an asteroid discovered the year before.
funFacts: A block of palladium can absorb 900 times its own volume of hydrogen gas.
Palladium is named after Pallas, an asteroid found just a year earlier.
Most gasoline cars have palladium in the exhaust to clean the fumes.
It is used in the tips of spark plugs and in dental crowns.
Palladium chemistry won the 2010 Nobel Prize for building complex molecules.

compounds.name: Palladium chloride
compounds.about: The workhorse of palladium chemistry; also used in plating.

compounds.name: Tetrakis palladium
compounds.about: A Nobel-winning catalyst for joining carbon atoms.

compounds.name: Palladium oxide
compounds.about: A black powder used in exhaust catalysts.

compounds.name: Palladium acetate
compounds.about: A widely used catalyst in making medicines.

compounds.name: Palladium hydride
compounds.about: What forms when palladium soaks up hydrogen.

compounds.name: Sodium tetrachloropalladate
compounds.about: Used in electroplating and catalysis.

compounds.name: Palladium on carbon
compounds.about: Powdered palladium on charcoal, a lab favorite.

compounds.name: Vysotskite
compounds.about: A rare mineral containing palladium.

compounds.name: Palladium fluoride
compounds.about: Unusual because it is magnetic.

compounds.name: Potassium hexachloropalladate
compounds.about: Used to purify palladium from other metals.

name: Silver
nameMeaning: From Old English seolfor; symbol Ag from Latin argentum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other element on the periodic table, and it reflects light better too, which is why mirrors are silvered. It also kills bacteria, so it turns up in bandages and sports socks. Silver's only weakness is that it tarnishes black in polluted air.
funFacts: Silver is the best conductor of electricity of any element.
Mirrors work because of a thin silver coating on the back of the glass.
Before digital cameras, every photograph was made using silver compounds.
Silver kills germs, so it is woven into socks and used in wound dressings.
The country Argentina is named after silver — argentum.

compounds.name: Silver nitrate
compounds.about: Stains skin black; used in medicine and photography.

compounds.name: Silver bromide
compounds.about: The light-sensitive crystal in photographic film.

compounds.name: Silver chloride
compounds.about: Turns purple-gray in sunlight; used in sensors.

compounds.name: Silver sulfide
compounds.about: The black tarnish that dulls silver spoons.

compounds.name: Silver oxide
compounds.about: Powers the tiny button batteries in watches.

compounds.name: Silver iodide
compounds.about: Sprayed into clouds to try to make rain.

compounds.name: Silver fluoride
compounds.about: Used by dentists to stop tooth decay spreading.

compounds.name: Silver carbonate
compounds.about: A yellow solid used in chemistry as an oxidizer.

compounds.name: Silver cyanide
compounds.about: Used in silver electroplating baths.

compounds.name: Pyrargyrite
compounds.about: A deep red 'ruby silver' ore mineral.

name: Cadmium
nameMeaning: From cadmia, the Latin name for zinc ore

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Cadmium gave painters some of the most brilliant yellows, oranges and reds ever made — Monet and Van Gogh both used cadmium paints. Unfortunately cadmium is also quite poisonous and builds up in the body, so today its use is carefully controlled.
funFacts: Cadmium yellow and cadmium red are famous artists' paint colors.
Cadmium is toxic and builds up in the body, so it is banned from most products.
Rechargeable NiCd batteries once powered nearly every cordless device.
Cadmium absorbs neutrons, so it is used in nuclear reactor control rods.
Cadmium selenide quantum dots make the pure colors in QLED televisions.

compounds.name: Cadmium sulfide
compounds.about: The brilliant cadmium yellow artists' pigment.

compounds.name: Cadmium selenide
compounds.about: Quantum dots that glow precise colors in TV screens.

compounds.name: Cadmium telluride
compounds.about: Used in a common type of thin-film solar panel.

compounds.name: Cadmium oxide
compounds.about: A brown powder used in electroplating.

compounds.name: Cadmium chloride
compounds.about: Used in photography and dyeing.

compounds.name: Cadmium hydroxide
compounds.about: The electrode material in NiCd batteries.

compounds.name: Cadmium sulfate
compounds.about: Used in standard cells that produce exact voltages.

compounds.name: Otavite
compounds.about: A rare cadmium carbonate mineral.

compounds.name: Cadmium red
compounds.about: The deep red version of the cadmium pigment.

compounds.name: Cadmium zinc telluride
compounds.about: Detects X-rays and gamma rays in scanners.

name: Indium
nameMeaning: From the indigo-blue line in its spectrum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Indium is a soft metal you can scratch with a fingernail, and it screams — a real crackling sound — when you bend it. Its most important job is invisible: a see-through indium coating on your phone screen is what lets the glass sense your finger.
funFacts: Bend a bar of indium and it makes a crackling 'tin cry' sound.
Every touchscreen has a transparent indium layer that senses your finger.
Indium is so soft you can leave a fingerprint in it.
It sticks to glass, so it is used to seal windows in vacuum equipment.
Indium stays soft even at extremely cold temperatures, so it seals space instruments.

compounds.name: Indium tin oxide
compounds.about: The see-through conductor on every touchscreen.

compounds.name: Indium phosphide
compounds.about: Powers the lasers that send data down fiber-optic cables.

compounds.name: Indium arsenide
compounds.about: Used in infrared and night-vision detectors.

compounds.name: Indium gallium nitride
compounds.about: The glowing layer inside blue and white LEDs.

compounds.name: Indium oxide
compounds.about: A yellow powder used in transparent coatings.

compounds.name: Indium chloride
compounds.about: Used to make other indium chemicals.

compounds.name: Indium antimonide
compounds.about: One of the best infrared detector materials.

compounds.name: Copper indium selenide
compounds.about: A flexible thin-film solar material.

compounds.name: Indium hydroxide
compounds.about: A step in refining indium from zinc ore.

compounds.name: Indium sulfide
compounds.about: A yellow-red solid used in solar cell layers.

name: Tin
nameMeaning: From Old English tin; symbol Sn from Latin stannum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Tin changed history: mix a little tin with copper and you get bronze, hard enough for tools and swords, which started the Bronze Age. Today tin coats steel cans to stop food going rusty, and tin solder holds together every circuit board in every gadget you own.
funFacts: The Bronze Age is named after copper mixed with tin.
Bend a bar of tin and it screeches — the famous 'tin cry'.
In freezing cold, tin crumbles into gray powder; this is called tin pest.
'Tin cans' are actually steel with a very thin tin coating inside.
Solder, which joins electronics together, is mostly tin.

compounds.name: Cassiterite
compounds.about: The main tin ore, and a coating on low-energy glass.

compounds.name: Tin(II) chloride
compounds.about: Used to silver mirrors and in dye-making.

compounds.name: Stannous fluoride
compounds.about: The tooth-protecting fluoride in some toothpastes.

compounds.name: Herzenbergite
compounds.about: A dark tin sulfide mineral.

compounds.name: Tin(IV) chloride
compounds.about: A fuming liquid used to coat glass.

compounds.name: Bronze
compounds.about: The copper-tin alloy that started an entire age of history.

compounds.name: Tin(II) oxide
compounds.about: A blue-black powder used in glass making.

compounds.name: Stannite
compounds.about: A tin-bearing ore mineral.

compounds.name: Tributyltin hydride
compounds.about: A lab reagent; related tin compounds once painted ship hulls.

compounds.name: Organotin stabilizers
compounds.about: Added to PVC plastic to stop it breaking down in sunlight.

name: Antimony
nameMeaning: From Greek anti + monos, 'not alone'; symbol Sb from stibium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Antimony has been used for over 5,000 years — ancient Egyptians ground it into kohl, the black eye make-up you see in tomb paintings. Today its main job is stopping fires: antimony compounds are mixed into plastics, mattresses and clothing to slow burning.
funFacts: Ancient Egyptian black eyeliner was made from an antimony mineral.
Antimony expands as it freezes, which made it perfect for sharp printing type.
It is a flame retardant found in mattresses, car seats and children's pajamas.
Antimony is a metalloid — it looks like a shiny metal but is brittle as glass.
Medieval alchemists were fascinated by it and wrote whole books about it.

compounds.name: Stibnite
compounds.about: The main ore, and the ancient Egyptian eye make-up.

compounds.name: Antimony trioxide
compounds.about: The world's most-used flame retardant.

compounds.name: Antimony trichloride
compounds.about: Once called 'butter of antimony' for its greasy look.

compounds.name: Indium antimonide
compounds.about: A superb infrared detector material.

compounds.name: Stibine
compounds.about: A poisonous gas used in the electronics industry.

compounds.name: Antimony pentoxide
compounds.about: A flame retardant and a catalyst.

compounds.name: Lead-antimony alloy
compounds.about: Makes car battery plates strong enough to last.

compounds.name: Antimony telluride
compounds.about: Converts heat into electricity in small coolers.

compounds.name: Tartar emetic
compounds.about: An old and rather brutal medicine.

compounds.name: Antimony pentafluoride
compounds.about: Part of the strongest acid ever made, called a superacid.

name: Tellurium

zhRadical.note: The 石 (stone) radical — this element is a solid nonmetal.

description: Tellurium has an embarrassing side effect: swallow the tiniest speck and your breath smells of garlic for weeks. It is rarer in the crust than gold. Its big modern use is in solar panels and in materials that turn heat straight into electricity.
funFacts: A microscopic amount of tellurium gives you garlic breath for weeks.
Tellurium is rarer in the Earth's crust than gold or platinum.
It is one of the few elements found combined with gold in nature.
Cadmium telluride solar panels are among the cheapest to make.
Named after the Earth, while its cousin selenium is named after the Moon.

compounds.name: Cadmium telluride
compounds.about: A leading thin-film solar panel material.

compounds.name: Bismuth telluride
compounds.about: Turns electricity into cooling in portable fridges.

compounds.name: Tellurium dioxide
compounds.about: Used in special glass that bends sound and light.

compounds.name: Calaverite
compounds.about: A gold ore mineral that also contains tellurium.

compounds.name: Hydrogen telluride
compounds.about: A gas that smells even worse than rotten eggs.

compounds.name: Zinc telluride
compounds.about: Used in solar cells and infrared devices.

compounds.name: Antimony telluride
compounds.about: A thermoelectric material used in coolers.

compounds.name: GST
compounds.about: Stores data on rewritable discs and in phase-change memory.

compounds.name: Tellurium tetrachloride
compounds.about: A white solid used in chemical synthesis.

compounds.name: Lead telluride
compounds.about: Generates electricity from heat in space probes.

name: Iodine

zhRadical.note: The 石 (stone) radical — this element is a solid nonmetal.

description: Iodine is a shiny purple-black solid that does something strange when warmed: it turns straight into a violet gas without ever becoming liquid. Your thyroid gland needs iodine to work, which is why it is added to table salt all over the world.
funFacts: Solid iodine turns directly into a purple gas — a process called sublimation.
Adding iodine to table salt has prevented illness in millions of people.
Iodine turns starch a dramatic blue-black, a classic school science test.
It was discovered by accident while making gunpowder from seaweed ash.
Iodine tincture was used to clean wounds long before modern antiseptics.

compounds.name: Potassium iodide
compounds.about: Added to table salt; also protects the thyroid after nuclear accidents.

compounds.name: Sodium iodide
compounds.about: A crystal that flashes when radiation hits it, used in detectors.

compounds.name: Silver iodide
compounds.about: Used in cloud seeding to encourage rainfall.

compounds.name: Iodine tincture
compounds.about: The brown antiseptic painted on skin before surgery.

compounds.name: Amiodarone
compounds.about: A heart medicine containing iodine.

compounds.name: Thyroxine
compounds.about: The thyroid hormone that controls how fast your body works.

compounds.name: Hydroiodic acid
compounds.about: One of the strongest acids there is.

compounds.name: Nitrogen triiodide
compounds.about: So unstable that a feather's touch makes it bang.

compounds.name: Potassium iodate
compounds.about: Another iodine source added to salt and flour.

compounds.name: Povidone-iodine
compounds.about: The orange-brown surgical scrub used in hospitals.

name: Xenon

zhRadical.note: The 气 (gas) radical — this element is a gas.

description: Xenon is the noble gas that broke the rules. Everyone believed noble gases could never form compounds, until 1962 when a chemist made one from xenon and shocked the world. Xenon also makes the dazzling blue-white light in car headlamps and camera flashes.
funFacts: In 1962 xenon proved that noble gases can react after all, rewriting the textbooks.
Xenon headlights and photo flashes give a brilliant daylight-white glow.
Ion engines on spacecraft push xenon out of the back to fly across the solar system.
Xenon can be used as an anesthetic to send patients to sleep.
It is so rare that xenon is only 0.00001% of the air.

compounds.name: Xenon difluoride
compounds.about: The first easy-to-make xenon compound; used to etch silicon.

compounds.name: Xenon tetrafluoride
compounds.about: Beautiful colorless crystals that stunned chemists in 1962.

compounds.name: Xenon hexafluoride
compounds.about: A yellow solid, the highest xenon fluoride.

compounds.name: Xenon trioxide
compounds.about: An explosive white solid — handle with great care.

compounds.name: Xenon tetroxide
compounds.about: So unstable it explodes above −36 °C.

compounds.name: Xenon hexafluoroplatinate
compounds.about: The very first noble gas compound ever made.

compounds.name: Sodium perxenate
compounds.about: One of the most powerful oxidizing agents known.

compounds.name: Xenon oxytetrafluoride
compounds.about: A colorless liquid used in fluorine chemistry.

compounds.name: Xenon chloride
compounds.about: A short-lived molecule that powers excimer lasers for eye surgery.

compounds.name: Xenon hydroxide hydride
compounds.about: A fragile molecule trapped in frozen ice for study.

name: Cesium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Cesium is the most reactive metal of all and one of only a few that melt in a warm room — a lump would turn to golden liquid in your hand, if it were not so dangerous to touch. Cesium atoms keep the world's time: the official length of one second is defined by cesium.
funFacts: The second is officially defined as 9,192,631,770 vibrations of a cesium atom.
Cesium melts at 28 °C, so it would be liquid on a hot day.
It is the most reactive metal — it explodes on contact with water, even ice.
Cesium is soft, gold-colored and one of only three golden metals with copper and gold.
Cesium clocks lose less than a second in 100 million years.

compounds.name: Cesium chloride
compounds.about: Used to spin DNA apart in laboratories.

compounds.name: Cesium carbonate
compounds.about: A useful base in making medicines.

compounds.name: Cesium hydroxide
compounds.about: One of the strongest bases known.

compounds.name: Cesium nitrate
compounds.about: Used in infrared flares that decoy missiles.

compounds.name: Cesium iodide
compounds.about: Flashes when X-rays hit it; used in medical scanners.

compounds.name: Cesium fluoride
compounds.about: A handy source of fluoride in chemistry.

compounds.name: Cesium formate
compounds.about: A very dense liquid used in deep oil drilling.

compounds.name: Cesium oxide
compounds.about: Used to coat surfaces that release electrons easily.

compounds.name: Pollucite
compounds.about: The mineral almost all cesium is mined from.

compounds.name: Cesium sulfate
compounds.about: Used to separate particles by spinning them fast.

name: Barium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Barium is a heavy metal whose salts are mostly poisonous — except one. Barium sulfate will not dissolve at all, so it passes safely through you, and doctors get patients to drink a 'barium meal' so their insides show up clearly on an X-ray.
funFacts: A 'barium meal' is a thick white drink that makes your gut visible on X-rays.
Barium compounds make the green colors in fireworks.
Its name means 'heavy' — barium minerals are noticeably weighty for their size.
Barium is so reactive it must be stored under oil.
Drilling for oil uses huge amounts of barium to weigh down drilling mud.

compounds.name: Barite
compounds.about: The safe 'barium meal' for X-rays, and a drilling mud weight.

compounds.name: Witherite
compounds.about: Used in making glass and ceramics; also rat poison.

compounds.name: Barium chloride
compounds.about: Colors flames green; used in fireworks.

compounds.name: Barium titanate
compounds.about: Generates electricity when squeezed; used in microphones.

compounds.name: Barium oxide
compounds.about: Used to dry gases and in special glass.

compounds.name: Barium nitrate
compounds.about: The green star in firework displays.

compounds.name: Barium ferrite
compounds.about: The ceramic magnets in speakers and fridge magnets.

compounds.name: Barium sulfide
compounds.about: An early glow-in-the-dark material.

compounds.name: Barium hydroxide
compounds.about: A strong base used in chemistry labs.

compounds.name: YBCO
compounds.about: A high-temperature superconductor containing barium.

name: Lanthanum

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Lanthanum's name means 'hidden', because it hid inside another element's ore for years before anyone noticed it. It is the first of the fifteen lanthanides, the row that sits below the main table. Lanthanum makes camera lenses sharper and helps hybrid car batteries store energy.
funFacts: Lanthanum gives its name to a whole family of fifteen elements.
Expensive camera lenses contain lanthanum glass, which bends light beautifully.
Hybrid car batteries can hold kilograms of lanthanum.
Despite being called a 'rare earth', it is more common than lead.
Lanthanum compounds help clean up phosphate from lakes and ponds.

compounds.name: Lanthanum oxide
compounds.about: Added to glass to make high-quality camera lenses.

compounds.name: Lanthanum nickel
compounds.about: Soaks up hydrogen; used in rechargeable batteries.

compounds.name: Lanthanum chloride
compounds.about: Used to make other lanthanum chemicals.

compounds.name: Lanthanum hexaboride
compounds.about: Shoots out electrons in electron microscopes.

compounds.name: Monazite
compounds.about: The main ore of lanthanum and other rare earths.

compounds.name: Lanthanum fluoride
compounds.about: Used in optical coatings and sensors.

compounds.name: Lanthanum carbonate
compounds.about: A medicine for kidney patients.

compounds.name: Lanthanum aluminate
compounds.about: A base crystal for growing superconductor films.

compounds.name: Lanthanum manganite
compounds.about: Changes resistance in a magnetic field.

compounds.name: Lanthanum oxysulfide

name: Cerium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Cerium is the most common of all the rare earth elements — there is more cerium in the ground than copper. Scratch it and it throws off sparks, which is exactly how the flint in a cigarette lighter works. It also cleans up exhaust fumes and polishes glass to a perfect shine.
funFacts: The sparking 'flint' in a lighter is mostly cerium alloy.
Cerium is more abundant in the crust than copper, tin or lead.
It is named after Ceres, discovered as an asteroid two years before the element.
Cerium oxide is the standard polish for making telescope and phone glass smooth.
It can breathe oxygen in and out, which is why car exhaust catalysts use it.

name: Praseodymium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Praseodymium means 'green twin' — for years it was mixed up with neodymium and the pair were thought to be one element called didymium. Its green salts color glass, and welders wear praseodymium goggles that block the fierce yellow glare of hot metal.
funFacts: Welders' and glassblowers' goggles use praseodymium to filter out the glare.
It was separated from its 'twin' neodymium only in 1885.
Praseodymium salts are a lovely apple green.
Mixed with nickel, it is one of the best materials for reaching ultra-low temperatures.
It goes into the powerful magnets in headphones and wind turbines.

name: Neodymium

zhRadical.note: The 钅(metal) radical — this element is a metal.

description: Neodymium makes the strongest permanent magnets ever invented — a coin-sized one can lift many kilograms and pinch your fingers hard. These magnets are hidden in headphones, phone speakers, hard drives, electric car motors and wind turbines all over the world.
funFacts: Neodymium magnets are so strong that big ones can break bones.
Every pair of headphones and every phone speaker contains a neodymium magnet.
A single wind turbine can hold hundreds of kilograms of neodymium.
Neodymium glass changes color depending on whether it is daylight or lamplight.
Powerful green laser pointers use a neodymium crystal to make their light.
